content: 1. Epidemiology of HSV-2 and HSV-1 Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) is the leading cause of genital ulcers in many countries. In 2012, approximately 20 million new HSV-2 infections occurred globally among individuals aged 15–49, with the highest rates observed in younger age groups. This translates to an estimated 417 million people living with HSV-2 infection worldwide. Despite lower prevalence rates, regions such as WHO South-East Asia and the Western Pacific harbor significant numbers of infected individuals due to their large populations. HSV-1, traditionally associated with oral herpes, is increasingly recognized as a cause of genital herpes, particularly in high-income countries, often transmitted through oral-genital contact. In 2012, an estimated 140 million people globally had genital HSV-1 infection. 2. HSV-2 and HIV Synergy HSV-2 is of particular concern due to its epidemiological synergy with HIV. Individuals infected with HSV-2 are approximately three times more likely to acquire HIV. Furthermore, those co-infected with HIV and HSV-2 are more likely to transmit HIV to others. In people living with HIV, HSV-2 infections are often more severe and can lead to rare but serious complications, such as infections of the brain, eyes, or lungs. 3. Clinical Presentation of HSV-2 HSV-2 is the most common cause of recurrent genital ulcer disease (GUD) worldwide. Symptomatic genital HSV is a lifelong condition characterized by frequent symptomatic recurrences. Most initial infections are asymptomatic or atypical, leading to underdiagnosis in the majority of cases. The classical presentation of primary genital HSV infection includes bilateral clusters of erythematous papules, vesicles, or ulcers on the external genitalia, perianal region, or buttocks, typically appearing 4–7 days after sexual exposure. However, this classical syndrome occurs in only 10–25% of primary infections. Symptoms include genital pain, itching, and dysuria (reported by 80% of women). Constitutional symptoms such as fever, headache, myalgias, and malaise are common. Cervicitis and tender inguinal or femoral lymphadenopathy often accompany initial infections. Over 2–3 weeks, lesions progress from vesicles to pustules, then coalesce into ulcers before crusting over and healing. Mucosal lesions may ulcerate without initially presenting as vesicles. Atypical presentations include small erosions, fissures, or dysuria/urethritis without visible lesions. 4. Recurrent HSV-2 Infections Most individuals with HSV-2 experience one or more symptomatic recurrences within a year of the first symptomatic episode. Recurrent episodes are generally less severe than the initial infection, with fewer lesions, unilateral presentation, and absence of systemic symptoms. Pain is less intense, and lesions typically heal within 5–10 days without antiviral treatment. Immunocompromised individuals, including those with HIV, experience more frequent and severe recurrences. Recurrent ulcers can cause significant physical and psychological morbidity. 5. Laboratory Diagnosis of HSV Genital HSV infection is often diagnosed clinically, but laboratory testing is required to differentiate between HSV-1 and HSV-2. When vesicles are absent, laboratory confirmation may be necessary to rule out other causes of genital ulcers. Diagnostic methods include direct detection from lesions (e.g., antigen detection, viral culture, nucleic acid amplification tests [NAATs] for viral DNA) and serological assays to detect type-specific antibodies, which develop within weeks of initial infection and persist indefinitely. 6. Rationale for Updated WHO Guidelines The 2003 WHO guidelines for genital HSV treatment require updates to address the changing epidemiology of HSV-2 and its synergy with HIV transmission. HSV-2 has become the most common cause of GUD in many countries. Updated global guidance on the optimal dose and duration of acyclovir treatment for symptomatic initial and recurrent episodes is essential. Recommendations for treating HSV-2 in people living with HIV, who experience more severe presentations, also need revision. Suppressive therapy has been shown to reduce both HIV and HSV-2 viral shedding and recurrences, and updated recommendations are needed to guide its use, particularly in areas with high HIV prevalence. 7. Objectives of the Guidelines The primary objectives of these guidelines are to provide evidence-based recommendations for the treatment of genital HSV infection and to support countries in updating their national treatment guidelines. 8. Target Audience These guidelines are intended for healthcare providers at all levels of the healthcare system, including those involved in sexual and reproductive health programs, such as HIV/AIDS, family planning, maternal and child health, and adolescent health. They are also relevant for policymakers, program managers, and other professionals responsible for implementing STI management interventions. 9. Structure of the Guidelines The guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for treating specific clinical conditions caused by genital HSV infection. They also offer direction for countries to develop national treatment recommendations, considering local antimicrobial resistance patterns, healthcare capacity, and resources. Updated treatment recommendations are included for common HSV-related conditions, while rare conditions (e.g., HSV meningoencephalitis) and neonatal HSV infections will be addressed in separate modules. 10. Development of the Guidelines The guidelines were developed following the 2014 WHO handbook for guideline development. A Guideline Development Group (GDG) comprising 33 international STI experts was established. The GDG identified key clinical questions and outcomes, conducted systematic reviews, and formulated recommendations based on the GRADE approach. Recommendations were finalized through consensus and peer-reviewed before publication. 11. Strength of Recommendations Recommendations are categorized as either strong or conditional. Strong recommendations use the wording The WHO STI guideline recommends… while conditional recommendations use The WHO STI guideline suggests…. The implications of these recommendations for patients, clinicians, and policymakers are detailed in the guidelines.
